title: One More Than the Root
statement: For each positive integer $n$, let $c(n)$ be the largest integer whose cube is at most $n$. How many positive integers $n$ with $n \le 5000$ are divisible by $c(n) + 1$?
hints: Fix a value $k$ of $c(n)$ and look at the block of all integers $n$ with $c(n) = k$. Within this block the divisor $c(n) + 1$ is the constant $k + 1$. Which integers does the block contain?

The block with $c(n) = k$ is $k^3 \le n < (k+1)^3$. Use modular arithmetic with modulus $k + 1$ to find the first and last multiples of $k + 1$ in the block: since $k \equiv -1 \pmod{k+1}$, we can read off the residue of $k^3$.

Since $k^3 \equiv -1 \pmod{k+1}$, the first multiple in the block is $k^3 + 1$, and the last is $(k+1)^3 - (k+1)$. Writing $n = (k+1)q$ gives $k^2 - k + 1 \le q \le k^2 + 2k$, which is $3k$ values of $q$. Because $17^3 = 4913 \le 5000 < 18^3$, the blocks $k = 1, \dots, 16$ are complete, and only the multiples of $18$ from $4914$ to $5000$ remain to be counted from the block $k = 17$.
solution: For a positive integer $k$, we have $c(n) = k$ exactly when $k^3 \le n < (k+1)^3$. These blocks, for $k \ge 1$, partition the positive integers. Within block $k$, we must count the multiples of $k + 1$. Since $k \equiv -1 \pmod{k+1}$, we have $k^3 \equiv -1 \pmod{k+1}$. As $k + 1 \ge 2$, this means $k^3$ is not a multiple of $k + 1$, but $k^3 + 1 = (k+1)(k^2 - k + 1)$ is, so $k^3 + 1$ is the first multiple in the block. The value $(k+1)^3$ lies just outside the block, so the last multiple is $(k+1)^3 - (k+1) = (k+1)(k^2 + 2k)$. Writing $n = (k+1)q$, the multiples in the block are exactly those with $k^2 - k + 1 \le q \le k^2 + 2k$. This gives $(k^2 + 2k) - (k^2 - k + 1) + 1 = 3k$ values of $q$. Now $17^3 = 4913 \le 5000 < 5832 = 18^3$, so the blocks $k = 1, \dots, 16$ lie entirely within the range $n \le 5000$, and they contribute $3(1 + 2 + \dots + 16) = 3 \cdot 136 = 408$ integers. The remaining integers are $4913 \le n \le 5000$, which all have $c(n) = 17$, so we need the multiples of $18$ among them. The first is $4914 = 18 \cdot 273$. Since $18 \cdot 277 = 4986 \le 5000 < 5004 = 18 \cdot 278$, the last is $18 \cdot 277$. So $q$ runs from $273$ to $277$, which gives $5$ integers. The answer is $408 + 5 = 413$. Why this works. modular-arithmetic, block-grouping-of-sums: on each block the divisor is constant, and working modulo $k + 1$ pins down the first and last multiples, so every complete block contributes exactly $3k$.
